\section[jadis]{jadis — long ago, in olden days}

\label{lesson:FR-C272-jadis}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the French for in the long run, then the French for sooner or later.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: jadis}
\textbf{jadis} — \textquotedblleft{}long ago, in olden days\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Jadis, cette rue était un marché.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Long ago, this street was a market.}
\end{quote}

Literary and a little old-fashioned; fairy tales like it.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{jadis} comes from Old French \emph{ja a dis} \textquotedblleft{}it is days already\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), with \emph{ja} from Latin \emph{iam} \textquotedblleft{}already\textquotedblright{} and \emph{dis} from Latin \emph{diēs} \textquotedblleft{}day\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{jadis}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{jadis}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the French for in the long run, then the French for sooner or later, then say \emph{jadis} again
\end{itemize}

\section[naguère]{naguère — not long ago; formerly (literary)}

\label{lesson:FR-C272-naguere}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the French for sooner or later, then the French for long ago.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: naguère}
\textbf{naguère} — \textquotedblleft{}not long ago; formerly (literary)\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Naguère, ce village était très calme.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Not long ago, this village was very quiet.}
\end{quote}

From \emph{n'a guère}: it is hardly (long) ago. Many writers now use it for 'formerly'.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{naguère} comes from \emph{n'a guère} \textquotedblleft{}it is hardly (long)\textquotedblright{}. \emph{Guère} is usually traced to a Frankish word meaning \textquotedblleft{}much\textquotedblright{}; the origin is not fully settled (EtymDB lists no parent).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{naguère}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{naguère}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{naguère}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the French for sooner or later, then the French for long ago, then say \emph{naguère} again
\end{itemize}

\section[auparavant]{auparavant — before, previously}

\label{lesson:FR-C272-auparavant}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the French for long ago, then the French for not long ago.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: auparavant}
\textbf{auparavant} — \textquotedblleft{}before, previously\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Elle est médecin; auparavant, elle était professeur.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{She is a doctor; before that, she was a teacher.}
\end{quote}

An adverb that stands alone. Before a noun, French uses \emph{avant}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{auparavant} is built from \emph{au}, \emph{par} and \emph{avant}; \emph{avant} is inherited from Late Latin \emph{abante}, built on Latin \emph{ante} \textquotedblleft{}before\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{auparavant}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{auparavant}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{auparavant}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the French for long ago, then the French for not long ago, then say \emph{auparavant} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\section[jusqu'alors]{jusqu'alors — until then, up to then}

\label{lesson:FR-C272-jusqu-alors}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the French for not long ago, then the French for before.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: jusqu'alors}
\textbf{jusqu'alors} — \textquotedblleft{}until then, up to then\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Jusqu'alors, personne ne connaissait son secret.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Until then, nobody knew his secret.}
\end{quote}

Looks back to a moment in the past; from today, say \emph{jusqu'à maintenant}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{jusque} is built on Latin \emph{ūsque} \textquotedblleft{}all the way\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short) with \emph{inde} (EtymDB) or, in another view, \emph{dē}; \emph{alors} joins \emph{à} and \emph{lors}, which EtymDB traces to Latin \emph{illā hōrā} \textquotedblleft{}at that hour\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{jusqu'alors}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{jusqu'alors}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{jusqu'alors}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the French for not long ago, then the French for before, then say \emph{jusqu'alors} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\section[depuis lors]{depuis lors — since then, ever since}

\label{lesson:FR-C272-depuis-lors}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the French for before, then the French for until then.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: depuis lors}
\textbf{depuis lors} — \textquotedblleft{}since then, ever since\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Il est parti en 2010; depuis lors, il n'écrit plus.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{He left in 2010; since then, he no longer writes.}
\end{quote}

Formal; in speech, \emph{depuis} or \emph{depuis ce moment-là}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{depuis} joins \emph{de} and \emph{puis} \textquotedblleft{}then\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB); \emph{lors} is traced in EtymDB to Latin \emph{illā hōrā} \textquotedblleft{}at that hour\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}

\raggedright

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{depuis lors}, once more

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the French for before, then the French for until then, then say \emph{depuis lors} again
\end{itemize}
